newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso sees deficit challenge ahead.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso sees deficit challenge ahead.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said his government's Real Plan to stabilize the economy had transformed Brazil, slashing inflation and reducing poverty, but he saw challenges ahead, mainly in reducing the budget deficit.
"Those who said the Real Plan was introduced for the rich were simply lying," Cardoso said in reference to a currency plan, introduced in July 1994, which dramatically slashed inflation.
Cardoso made the staements in an end-of-year speech to his cabinet that was broadcast on radio and television.

The president, armed with charts and graphs, reminded his ministers of official figures showing how 13 million Brazilians clawed their way out of poverty since 1994, when the Real Plan was introduced.

Cardoso also recalled Finance Ministry projections of 30 percent growth in gross domestic product between 1993 and 1998 and its expectation of a one-trillion-dollar economy by the turn of the century.

Per capita income was projected to double to about $6,000 a year by 2000 and consumer trends had already been altered beyond recognition from a couple of years ago, with growth seen in sales across the market, from automobiles to yogurt.
"We're talking about changes in the living standards of the population," Cardoso said. "This could only happen because there has been better wealth distribution."
"We have had and we still have problems with the (budget) deficit," the president said in his speech.

Brazil's operational deficit in 1996 is expected to be equivalent to about four percent of GDP, 1.5 percentage points higher than an original target. The government hopes a package of cost-cutting measures in the federal sector will keep the deficit to 2.5 percent in 1997.

Cardoso urged Congress to press ahead with approving two reforms considered crucial to curbing public spending -- one to allow wide job cuts in the civil service and the other to balance the social security system which went into the red in November.
"I make an appeal to the (party) leaders -- the reforms are fundamental. Without them we won't have clear horizons regarding the public deficit," he said.
